message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2026) Below is a concise overview of the most important rights you have as a renter in Texas. These rights are derived from the Texas Property Code, local ordinances, and federal law. While the list is comprehensive, it’s not exhaustive—always check the latest statutes or consult a qualified attorney if you have a specific situation. | Category | Key Rights | Practical Tips | |----------|------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **$1,000** for a single‑unit residential lease.
• Deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Get a written receipt.
• Ask for a move‑in inspection checklist. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• You can withhold rent only if the landlord fails to fix major problems after notice. | • Document problems with photos and written notice.
• Keep copies of all communications. | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually **24 hrs** for non‑emergency visits; **12 hrs** for emergencies).
• Landlord cannot enter without notice unless it’s an emergency. | • Ask for a written notice schedule.
• Keep a log of all entries. | | **Lease Terms** | • All lease terms must be **written** if the lease is longer than **one year**.
• You can negotiate terms (e.g., pet fees, subletting). | • Read the lease carefully before signing.
• Ask for clarification on any ambiguous clause. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on rent increases, but **notice** must be given:
 – For month‑to‑month leases: **30 days** notice.
 – For fixed‑term leases: increase only at the start of a new term. | • Ask for a written notice of any increase. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the **Texas Property Code §92.001–92.006**.
• Typical steps: notice to cure (30 days for non‑payment), notice of termination (30 days for other breaches), court filing, and a hearing. | • If you receive an eviction notice, respond promptly.
• Attend the hearing; you can present evidence of payment or repairs. | | **Discrimination** | • Protected under the **Fair Housing Act** and Texas’ own anti‑discrimination laws. Landlords cannot refuse to rent or impose different terms based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income. | • Keep records of any discriminatory remarks or actions. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major problem after notice, you may:
 1. Pay for the repair and deduct the cost from rent (up to the amount of the repair).
 2. Withhold rent (only after giving notice and following the proper procedure). | • Get a written estimate for the repair.
• Keep receipts and proof of payment. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • You may sublet or assign the lease only with the landlord’s **written consent** (unless the lease explicitly allows it). | • Ask for a written agreement if you plan to sublet. | | **Move‑Out Notice** | • For month‑to‑month leases, you must give **30 days** written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, you must either finish the term or negotiate a release. | • Provide a forwarding address for the return of your security deposit. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If the landlord violates your rights, you can file a claim in **small‑claims court** (up to $20,000) or pursue a civil suit. | • Gather all documentation: lease, receipts, correspondence, photos. | --- #### Quick Reference Checklist 1. **Security Deposit** – Verify amount, get receipt, know the 30‑day return rule. 2. **Move‑In Inspection** – Complete a checklist; note existing damage. 3. **Notice Requirements** – Landlord must give 24 hrs notice for entry (12 hrs for emergencies). 4. **Repair Requests** – Submit in writing; keep copies. 5. **Rent Payment** – Keep proof of payment (bank statements, receipts). 6. **Eviction Notice** – Respond within the time frame; attend the hearing. 7. **Discrimination Claims** – Report to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or Texas Attorney General. --- #### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Property Code** | Full statutory text (online via Texas Legislature website). | | **Texas Attorney General – Fair Housing** | Guidance on discrimination complaints. | | **HUD – Fair Housing** | Federal enforcement and complaint filing. | | **Texas Small Claims Court** | Information on filing a claim for damages or deposit disputes. | | **Local Tenant Associations** | Many cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas, Houston) have tenant advocacy groups. | | **Legal Aid Organizations** | Free or low‑cost legal help for tenants (e.g., Texas Legal Services Center). | --- #### When to Seek Legal Help - **Unresolved Repairs** after repeated notices. - **Discriminatory Treatment** or harassment. - **Unlawful Eviction** or improper notice. - **Large Security Deposit Deductions** that you believe are unjustified. - **Complex Lease Disputes** (e.g., subletting, lease termination). --- **Bottom Line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, privacy, fair treatment, and a clear, written lease. If a landlord violates these rights, you have legal avenues to protect yourself. Always keep thorough records and act promptly when issues arise.
